statements.text: Amphotericin B binds ergosterol in susceptible fungal membranes, increasing permeability and causing leakage of intracellular contents.
Fungicidal activity is concentration and organism dependent; liposomal delivery changes tissue distribution and toxicity relative to conventional amphotericin B.
Fungicidal activity is concentration and organism dependent; liposomal delivery changes tissue distribution and toxicity relative to conventional amphotericin B.

Label indications include empiric therapy in febrile neutropenia, cryptococcal meningitis in HIV, infections refractory/intolerant to conventional amphotericin B, and visceral leishmaniasis in specified patients.
Common reactions include fever, chills, nausea, vomiting, anemia, dyspnea, and infusion-related reactions.
Common reactions include chills/rigors, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dyspnea, rash, and infusion-related symptoms; frequency varies by indication and comparator.
Laboratory abnormalities commonly include increased creatinine/BUN, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, and liver-test abnormalities.
Serious risks include nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia, severe infusion or anaphylactoid reactions, hepatic toxicity, and blood dyscrasias.
Nephrotoxicity remains clinically important despite lower rates than conventional amphotericin B in comparative studies; renal function and electrolytes require serial monitoring.
Infusion reactions can include severe chest or back pain, flushing, hypotension, dyspnea, hypoxia, and tachycardia; they may improve when the infusion is stopped and restarted more slowly.

Serious less-common reactions include anaphylaxis, arrhythmia/cardiac arrest, hepatic failure, blood dyscrasias, seizures/encephalopathy, and pulmonary toxicity with simultaneous leukocyte transfusion.
Contraindicated in patients with demonstrated hypersensitivity to amphotericin B or formulation components unless the condition is life-threatening and requires treatment.
Administer by controlled IV infusion, manage acute infusion reactions, and do not substitute another amphotericin formulation without rechecking dose and product instructions.
The mean within-interval half-life is about 7 to 10 hours, while sampling through 49 days shows a terminal half-life of about 100 to 153 hours, probably reflecting slow tissue redistribution.
Metabolic pathways of amphotericin B after liposomal administration are not known.
Excretion of amphotericin B after the liposomal product has not been directly studied; clearance at steady state was independent of dose in the studied range.
Liposomal amphotericin B has nonlinear, formulation-specific pharmacokinetics and tissue distribution; it is not interchangeable milligram-for-milligram with other amphotericin products.
Liposomal amphotericin B has nonlinear pharmacokinetics between 1 and 5 mg/kg/day, with more-than-proportional increases in total serum concentration as dose rises.
Steady state is generally reached within four days, and stable trough concentrations across repeated dosing suggest no significant serum accumulation at a fixed dose.
Other nephrotoxins, corticosteroids/ACTH or potassium-wasting drugs, digoxin, flucytosine, and leukocyte transfusions can create clinically important additive risks.
Monitor renal and hepatic function, potassium, magnesium, CBC, infusion reactions, and clinical/mycologic response.
Adequate controlled pregnancy studies are unavailable; animal studies found no teratogenicity at studied exposures, but the product should be used only when potential benefit outweighs risk.
It is unknown whether amphotericin B is excreted in human milk; the label calls for a decision to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug because serious infant reactions are possible.
The effect of renal impairment on liposomal amphotericin B disposition has not been studied, although the product has been used in patients with pre-existing renal impairment.
The effect of hepatic impairment on liposomal amphotericin B disposition is unknown.
Patients 1 month to 16 years have been treated at adult-comparable mg/kg doses without an identified efficacy or safety difference; safety below one month is not established.
Experience in 72 patients age 65 or older did not require an age-based dosage change, but geriatric dosing still requires clinical assessment.
Overdose may cause cardiorespiratory arrest and severe organ toxicity; stop treatment and provide intensive supportive monitoring.
Polyene binding to ergosterol explains membrane pore formation; liposomal amphotericin B must stay formulation-specific when teaching nephrotoxicity and dosing.

statements.text: Binds penicillin-binding proteins and inhibits bacterial cell-wall peptidoglycan cross-linking, causing lysis of susceptible organisms.

Time-dependent bactericidal activity; beta-lactamases can inactivate ampicillin unless susceptibility or an appropriate inhibitor combination is present.
Indicated for susceptible respiratory, genitourinary, gastrointestinal, meningitic, septicemic, and endocardial infections as specified by organism and susceptibility.
Common reactions include rash, urticaria, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and injection-site reactions.
Gastrointestinal reactions include glossitis, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, enterocolitis, pseudomembranous colitis, and diarrhea; many are more often associated with oral dosage forms.
statements.scope: Ampicillin products; oral-form predominance explicitly retained

statements.text: Skin rash and urticaria are frequent hypersensitivity manifestations; serum-sickness-like reactions, erythema multiforme, and exfoliative dermatitis are also reported.
Serious risks include anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reactions, C. difficile-associated diarrhea, seizures at high exposure, blood dyscrasias, and hepatic injury.
Anaphylaxis is the most serious reaction and is particularly associated with parenteral therapy; it requires immediate epinephrine, airway/oxygen support, and other emergency treatment.
Hematologic reactions include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, eosinophilia, and agranulocytosis and are usually reversible after discontinuation.

Seizures and linear IgA bullous dermatosis are reported rare clinically important reactions; risk of neurotoxicity rises when beta-lactam exposure is excessive, particularly with impaired elimination.
Contraindicated in patients with prior serious hypersensitivity to ampicillin or other penicillins; cross-reactivity with other beta-lactams requires assessment.
Obtain allergy history, discontinue for serious hypersensitivity, use only for proven/strongly suspected susceptible bacteria, and adjust dosing for renal impairment.
In neonates younger than 28 days, ampicillin half-life decreases as postmenstrual age rises because renal function matures.
statements.scope: Ampicillin sodium for injection in neonates

statements.text: Ampicillin is excreted largely unchanged in urine; probenecid delays its renal excretion.
Parenteral ampicillin distributes broadly and is eliminated mainly by the kidney; probenecid delays renal tubular secretion.
Parenteral ampicillin distributes readily into most tissues and fluids; CSF and brain penetration becomes clinically meaningful when meninges are inflamed.
Ampicillin is about 20% protein-bound, lower than many other penicillins, and active drug appears in bile at concentrations higher than serum.
Probenecid raises and prolongs ampicillin concentrations; allopurinol increases rash frequency; aminoglycosides may be synergistic clinically but should not be physically mixed in the same solution.
Monitor cultures/susceptibility, renal/hepatic/hematologic function during prolonged therapy, allergic reactions, diarrhea, and neurologic toxicity in renal impairment.
Animal studies did not show harm at multiples of the human dose, but adequate controlled human pregnancy studies are unavailable; use only if clearly needed.
Ampicillin is excreted in trace amounts in human milk; administer cautiously to a nursing woman.
The label provides pediatric and neonatal dosing, and emphasizes that neonatal disposition changes with postmenstrual age and renal maturation.
High beta-lactam exposure can cause neuromuscular hyperirritability or seizures, especially with renal impairment; provide supportive care and renal dose correction.
Ampicillin is an aminopenicillin vulnerable to beta-lactamase; inhibitor combinations and enterococcal synergy are classic exam contexts, but product/susceptibility details matter.

statements.text: Reduces central cholinergic activity and helps restore dopaminergic-cholinergic balance in the striatum; it is not a dopamine-releasing drug.

Improves rigidity and tremor more than bradykinesia and relieves many acute dystonic/extrapyramidal reactions; it does not treat tardive dyskinesia.

Common anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, nausea, tachycardia, urinary retention, and cognitive impairment.
Anticholinergic gastrointestinal effects include dry mouth, nausea, vomiting, constipation, and potentially paralytic ileus.
Ocular and urinary effects include blurred vision, mydriasis, dysuria, and urinary retention; tachycardia may occur.
Serious risks include hyperthermia/anhidrosis, paralytic ileus, toxic psychosis/confusion, angle-closure glaucoma precipitation, and severe urinary retention.

Impaired sweating can lead to fever, hyperthermia, or heat stroke, especially in hot environments or during concurrent anticholinergic therapy.
Allergic skin rash is reported and requires discontinuation if it cannot be controlled by dose reduction.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity and in children younger than 3 years; use is hazardous in angle-closure glaucoma and obstructive urinary/GI disease.
Avoid treating tardive dyskinesia because symptoms may worsen; use caution in older adults, glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy, alcoholism, and hot environments.
The selected label describes a long duration of action that can persist through the night after bedtime dosing.
The selected label does not provide a modern detailed pharmacokinetic section sufficient for a verified quantitative summary.
Other anticholinergic or antidopaminergic drugs can intensify adverse effects; combining with tricyclic antidepressants, phenothiazines, or related agents increases anticholinergic toxicity.
Monitor cognition, vision/ocular symptoms, bowel and bladder function, temperature/sweating, heart rate, and whether the movement disorder is tardive dyskinesia rather than acute EPS.
Safe use of benztropine during pregnancy has not been established.
Benztropine is contraindicated below age 3 because of atropine-like toxicity and should be used cautiously in older children.

Overdose produces central and peripheral anticholinergic syndrome with agitation, delirium, mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia, urinary retention, and ileus; treatment is supportive/toxicology guided.
Benztropine helps tremor/rigidity and acute drug-induced EPS, but can worsen urinary retention and should not be used for tardive dyskinesia.

Produces temporary, localized reduction of muscle activity after injection; systemic spread can cause generalized botulinum effects.

Contraindicated with hypersensitivity to botulinum toxin products/components or infection at the proposed injection site.
Use the exact product-specific units, anatomy, and dosing; take special care in neuromuscular disorders and patients with baseline swallowing or breathing difficulty.
Conventional circulating pharmacokinetic measurements are not considered useful at recommended intramuscular doses; clinical effect duration is product and indication specific.
With currently available analytical methods, DAXXIFY cannot be detected in peripheral blood after intramuscular administration at the recommended dose.
Aminoglycosides or other agents interfering with neuromuscular transmission, anticholinergics, muscle relaxants, and recent botulinum toxin exposure can potentiate effects.
Monitor swallowing, speech, breathing, generalized weakness, ocular protection, and clinical response; counsel patients to seek urgent care for distant-spread symptoms.

statements.scope: DAXXIFY only; do not generalize to every botulinum toxin product

DAXXIFY trials found no increase in treatment-related adverse events among participants over 65, but enrolled numbers were insufficient to determine whether response differs from younger adults.

Excess effect may be delayed and cause generalized neuromuscular weakness or respiratory failure; observe and provide supportive/ventilatory care, with public-health antitoxin consultation when appropriate.
The core exam mechanism is SNAP-25 cleavage with failure of acetylcholine vesicle release; it causes flaccid rather than spastic paralysis.

Produces rapid, potent diuresis; excessive dosing can cause profound volume and electrolyte depletion.

Dose-related laboratory abnormalities include hyperuricemia, hypochloremia, hypokalemia, azotemia, hyponatremia, increased creatinine, and hyperglycemia.

Ototoxicity is a particular risk with high, repeated IV doses in impaired renal excretion and may be potentiated by other ototoxic drugs such as aminoglycosides.
Rare serious reactions include thrombocytopenia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, impaired hearing, and renal failure.
Boxed warning: bumetanide is a potent diuretic that can cause profound diuresis with water and electrolyte depletion; careful supervision and individualized dosing are required.
Contraindicated in anuria, hepatic coma, severe electrolyte depletion until corrected, and hypersensitivity.

After oral bumetanide, diuresis begins within 30 to 60 minutes and peak activity occurs in about 1 to 2 hours.
Bumetanide is a rapid-onset, short-duration loop diuretic; inadequate oral response may be reassessed after four to five hours before a subsequent dose.
Adult bumetanide elimination half-life is approximately 1 to 1.5 hours; neonatal half-life is much longer and falls rapidly during the first month of life as renal and hepatobiliary function mature.
Identified urinary and biliary bumetanide metabolites arise from oxidation of the N-butyl side chain.
After radiolabeled oral dosing, 81% of radioactivity was recovered in urine, including 45% as unchanged bumetanide; biliary excretion was about 2%.
Bumetanide has high oral bioavailability and short duration; renal and nonrenal elimination contribute, with altered handling in renal/hepatic disease.
In older volunteers, total clearance was lower and peak concentration higher than in younger adults, although bioavailability and volume of distribution were similar.
Aminoglycosides or other ototoxins, nephrotoxins, lithium, digoxin in hypokalemia, NSAIDs, and antihypertensives can create important additive risks.
Monitor weight, intake/output, blood pressure, renal function, sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, magnesium, uric acid, glucose, and hearing when risk is high.
Animal studies did not show teratogenicity or embryocidal effects at very high exposure multiples, but adequate controlled pregnancy studies are unavailable; use only if benefit justifies fetal risk.
It is unknown whether bumetanide is excreted in human milk; the selected label advises that nursing generally should not be undertaken during treatment.
Renal impairment increases concern for excessive diuresis and IV ototoxicity; treatment requires close renal-function, volume, and electrolyte monitoring.

Older adults have lower clearance and attenuated urine/sodium response; cautious dosing and renal monitoring are appropriate because renal function commonly declines with age.
Overdose causes excessive diuresis, dehydration, electrolyte depletion, hypotension, and circulatory collapse; replace fluid/electrolytes and provide supportive care.
Bumetanide is a loop diuretic; the exam triad is potent diuresis, hypokalemic/metabolic-alkalosis risk, and ototoxicity—while potassium-sparing agents cause hyperkalemia.

Biliary or urinary ceftriaxone-calcium precipitation can appear as gallbladder sludge/pseudolithiasis or renal calculi, especially in pediatric or severely ill patients.

Serious risks include anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reactions, C. difficile-associated diarrhea, immune hemolytic anemia, biliary sludge/pseudolithiasis, pancreatitis, seizures, and renal precipitation.
Serious or fatal beta-lactam hypersensitivity and anaphylaxis can occur and require immediate discontinuation and emergency treatment.
Neonates exposed to ceftriaxone and calcium-containing IV solutions have had fatal crystalline precipitates in lungs and kidneys; the neonatal calcium contraindication is product-critical.
Neurologic toxicity includes encephalopathy, seizures, myoclonus, and non-convulsive status epilepticus, particularly with excessive exposure in renal impairment.

Rare reactions include agranulocytosis, hemolytic anemia, pancreatitis, severe cutaneous reactions including SJS/TEN/AGEP, acute kidney injury from urinary precipitation, and Clostridioides difficile colitis.

Contraindicated in premature neonates, hyperbilirubinemic neonates, neonates requiring IV calcium-containing solutions, and patients with serious cephalosporin hypersensitivity; lidocaine-containing IM diluent has separate restrictions.
Never mix or simultaneously administer with IV calcium-containing solutions in neonates; monitor for hypersensitivity, hemolysis, biliary/urinary precipitation, and neurologic toxicity.
Middle-ear fluid concentrations in pediatric otitis media remained measurable through 48 hours, with a calculated middle-ear-fluid half-life around 25 hours in the cited study.

statements.text: Across 0.15 to 3 g in healthy adults, ceftriaxone elimination half-life ranged from approximately 5.8 to 8.7 hours; the mean was longer in older adults and renal impairment.
About 33% to 67% of a ceftriaxone dose is excreted unchanged in urine; the remainder is secreted into bile and reaches feces as microbiologically inactive compounds.
Ceftriaxone is not removed to a clinically significant extent by hemodialysis; combined severe renal and hepatic dysfunction requires close concentration/safety monitoring.
Ceftriaxone is highly protein bound and eliminated by both renal and biliary routes; it penetrates inflamed meninges.
Ceftriaxone distributes widely and penetrates inflamed meninges; in pediatric meningitis studies, CSF concentrations were measurable after 50 or 75 mg/kg IV doses.
Calcium-containing IV solutions are the critical compatibility interaction; anticoagulant effect and nephrotoxicity risks require context-specific review.
Monitor cultures, clinical response, CBC, renal/hepatic function during prolonged therapy, bilirubin in neonates, diarrhea, and biliary/urinary symptoms.
Animal studies did not show embryo-fetal toxicity at studied doses, but adequate controlled pregnancy studies are unavailable; use only if clearly needed.
Low ceftriaxone concentrations are excreted in human milk; administer cautiously to a nursing woman.

Pharmacokinetics are only minimally altered in isolated renal impairment and usual doses up to 2 g/day generally need no adjustment; severe combined renal and hepatic dysfunction is a separate high-risk scope.
Isolated hepatic dysfunction minimally alters ceftriaxone pharmacokinetics, but combined significant hepatic and renal dysfunction requires caution and monitoring.

Pediatric safety and effectiveness are established for labeled doses, but hyperbilirubinemic neonates and neonates requiring calcium-containing IV solutions have specific contraindications because of displacement and precipitation risks.
Geriatric pharmacokinetics are only minimally altered and doses up to 2 g/day generally require no age-only adjustment when severe combined renal/hepatic dysfunction is absent.
Overdose can increase neurologic and hematologic toxicity; treatment is supportive because dialysis does not efficiently remove ceftriaxone.
Ceftriaxone is third-generation, penetrates CSF, treats gonorrhea, and has a distinctive neonatal bilirubin/calcium-precipitation warning.

statements.text: Binds 23S rRNA of the 50S subunit and inhibits peptide-chain initiation/elongation; erm-mediated rRNA methylation can cause macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin B resistance.
Usually bacteriostatic at clinically achieved concentrations, with activity against many gram-positive aerobes and anaerobes but poor activity against aerobic gram-negative bacilli.
Usually bacteriostatic at clinically achieved concentrations, with activity against many gram-positive aerobes and anaerobes but poor activity against aerobic gram-negative bacilli.
Indicated for serious susceptible infections including selected lower respiratory, skin/soft tissue, gynecologic, intra-abdominal, septicemic, and bone/joint infections.
Common reactions include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, rash, and esophagitis/esophageal ulcer with capsules.

Gastrointestinal reactions include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and metallic/unpleasant taste; esophagitis or esophageal ulcer can occur when capsules are taken with too little water or while lying down.
Morbilliform rash is the most frequently reported hypersensitivity reaction; pruritus, urticaria, vaginitis, and angioedema also occur.
Serious risks include C. difficile-associated diarrhea/colitis, anaphylaxis, severe cutaneous reactions, hepatotoxicity, neutropenia/thrombocytopenia, and severe esophageal injury.
Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis can be severe or fatal and may begin during therapy or weeks after discontinuation.
Anaphylactic shock, DRESS, toxic epidermal necrolysis, AGEP, erythema multiforme/SJS-like reactions, and cutaneous vasculitis are reported severe hypersensitivity reactions.
Acute kidney injury and clinically important jaundice/liver-test abnormalities have been reported.
Hematologic reports include neutropenia, eosinophilia, agranulocytosis, and thrombocytopenia; causal attribution is not established for every report.
Boxed warning: clindamycin can cause severe, potentially fatal C. difficile-associated diarrhea/colitis and should be reserved for serious infections when less toxic agents are inappropriate.
Contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to clindamycin or lincomycin.
Evaluate significant diarrhea during and after treatment; use with caution in gastrointestinal disease, hepatic impairment, allergy, and neuromuscular disease.
After oral clindamycin hydrochloride, mean peak serum concentration is reached in approximately 45 minutes.
Average biologic half-life is approximately 2.4 hours; oral half-life averages about 4 hours in older adults and is slightly prolonged in marked renal or hepatic dysfunction.
Clindamycin is metabolized predominantly by CYP3A4 and to a lesser extent CYP3A5 to clindamycin sulfoxide and N-desmethyl clindamycin.
About 10% of bioactivity is excreted in urine and 3.6% in feces; the remainder is eliminated as inactive metabolites.
Oral clindamycin is well absorbed and widely distributed but does not reliably reach therapeutic cerebrospinal-fluid concentrations; hepatic metabolism and biliary/renal excretion contribute.
Multiple oral dosing for up to 14 days showed no evidence of accumulation or altered metabolism.
Clindamycin has neuromuscular-blocking properties and can enhance neuromuscular blockers; erythromycin can be antagonistic and inducible clindamycin resistance should be assessed when relevant.
Monitor clinical/culture response, diarrhea for weeks after therapy, liver and renal function during prolonged treatment, CBC when indicated, and swallowing/esophageal symptoms.

Systemic clindamycin during the second and third trimesters was not associated with an increased congenital-abnormality frequency in cited trials; first-trimester controlled data are inadequate, so use only if clearly needed.

Clindamycin appears in human milk at less than 0.5 to 3.8 mcg/mL; breastfeeding need not automatically stop, but monitor the infant for diarrhea, candidiasis, or rarely blood in stool/antibiotic-associated colitis.
Marked renal impairment slightly prolongs elimination half-life, but hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis do not effectively remove clindamycin.
Moderate-to-severe hepatic disease prolongs clindamycin half-life; accumulation is uncommon with every-eight-hour dosing, but periodic liver tests are recommended in severe disease.
Pediatric use from birth to 16 years requires appropriate organ-system monitoring; capsules are unsuitable for children unable to swallow them whole.
Age alone does not materially change IV clindamycin disposition, but oral half-life is longer in older adults; clinical studies were insufficient to define an overall differential geriatric response.
Overdose management is supportive; hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis do not effectively remove clindamycin.
Clindamycin binds 50S/23S rRNA and covers many anaerobes/gram-positive organisms; the defining safety issue is C. difficile colitis.
